I’m 49, I’ve farmed these lands around Quzhou for 25 years, and I know every mu of my 200 mu farm. With just my wife and me, I have to be smart — machinery does the heavy work, but I still make the decisions. I have well irrigation, so water is there if I pay for the diesel to pump it.

My bread and butter is the wheat-maize double crop. That rotation is reliable, fully mechanized, and the dealers come right to my gate. I’ll put 130 mu into that system. My winter wheat is already in the ground; now it’s greening up and I need to push it. I’ll topdress nitrogen and irrigate three times — green-up, jointing, and heading — and spray twice for powdery mildew and aphids. I always plant improved wheat seed; the hybrids don’t pay off here like they do for maize. After harvest in early June, I won’t waste a single day. I’ll plant hybrid maize right behind the combine, mostly no-tillage to save time and moisture. Two irrigations — one at tasseling and one at grain filling — and two sprays is all it needs if the weather cooperates. I expect about 500 kg/mu from the wheat and 600 kg/mu from the maize.

I keep 40 mu for millet. I plant it in May on ground that isn’t in the double-crop rotation. Millet doesn’t eat fertilizer like maize does, and it can handle a dry spell better. Two irrigations and one spray is enough. An improved millet seed gives me around 300 kg/mu, and the price has been decent lately.

The remaining 30 mu goes to autumn cabbage. Cabbage is where I make my cash, but it’s also where I sweat the most. I deep-plough that ground in summer and plant in late July. Cabbage is hungry — it needs plenty of N, P, and especially K. I’ll irrigate four times because heads won’t form right if they go thirsty, and I’ll spray three times to keep cabbage worms and aphids from ruining me. A good hybrid cabbage should pull 4,000 kg/mu if I stay on top of it.

This mix keeps me fed if grain prices drop, but doesn’t gamble my whole year on vegetables my wife and I can’t manage alone.
